narrative:
The model estimated a 26% probability that you would be a bad credit risk. In practical terms, among applicants with a similar profile, about one in four would be expected to have repayment problems. That risk level was above the lender’s acceptance threshold, so your application was denied.

The decision was shaped most strongly by three factors, in this order: your savings position, your checking-account status, and an existing installment plan with a bank. Your savings were recorded as unknown or none, and this was the single most influential factor; in your case it actually leaned toward good credit, and it is not unusual among approved applicants. Your checking-account status was also recorded as none, and it was the second most influential factor, again leaning toward good credit; this is common among approved applicants. The third factor, having an installment plan with a bank, was the strongest of the top three pushing toward bad credit, and only a small minority of approved applicants have this. The rest of your profile, including a 48-month term and a 3,914 DM request that are above approved averages, added further risk.

To improve your chances, reduce the requested amount or shorten the term, build a documented savings history, and settle or consolidate the bank installment plan before reapplying. You can also ask the lender whether missing savings or checking information can be updated, and seek credit counseling to address the combined risk factors.
